goal_name: Prepare for Database Systems Final Exam
goal_description: Review all topics: ER model, relational model, SQL, normalization, storage, and security. Final exam is 90 minutes MCQ + written, worth 50% of grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Review the ER model and its extended versions — practice designing conceptual schemas that satisfy data requirements of given applications.
Task 2: Study the relational data model — practice converting ER diagrams into relational schemas.
Task 3: Practice writing SQL statements: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), stored procedures, functions, and triggers.
Task 4: Practice identifying functional dependencies and keys for given relations.
Task 5: Determine normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) for relations given their primary key and functional dependencies.
Task 6: Review database storage concepts: physical data storage, indexing techniques, and approaches for managing large-scale data.
Task 7: Study database security: DAC and MAC access control, information flow control, and user management in MySQL/Oracle/MS SQL Server.
Task 8: Complete two past MCQ + written practice exams under 90-minute time conditions.

goal_description: Implement and manage a database application on MySQL covering schema creation, SQL queries, stored procedures, triggers, and basic user authorization. Lab component is 30% of total grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Install and configure MySQL locally and verify the connection.
Task 2: Translate the provided ER diagram into a relational schema and create all tables with appropriate constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL).
Task 3: Write DDL statements to define the full database schema.
Task 4: Write DML queries covering all required operations: multi-table SELECT with JOINs, subqueries, GROUP BY, HAVING, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
Task 5: Implement the required stored procedures and functions in SQL.
Task 6: Write and test triggers for the specified business rules.
Task 7: Implement basic authorization: create users, grant and revoke privileges using DCL statements.
Task 8: Prepare the lab report documenting schema design decisions and testing evidence.
Task 9: Submit the lab report at the end of the lab session as required.

goal_description: Deeply understand functional dependencies, keys, and normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) and be able to apply normalization algorithms to any relation.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Study the definition and rules for identifying functional dependencies in a relation.
Task 2: Practice finding the key(s) of a relation given a set of functional dependencies — including candidate keys and primary keys.
Task 3: Learn the definition of 1NF and identify violations (repeating groups, non-atomic attributes).
Task 4: Learn 2NF — identify and resolve partial dependencies on the primary key.
Task 5: Learn 3NF — identify and resolve transitive dependencies.
Task 6: Learn BCNF — identify relations where a non-trivial dependency's left side is not a superkey and decompose accordingly.
Task 7: Practice the decomposition algorithms: lossless-join decomposition and dependency-preserving decomposition.
Task 8: Solve at least 10 normalization exercises from the textbook (Elmasri & Navathe, 7th edition, Chapter on Functional Dependencies).
Task 9: Review normalization questions from previous final exams.

goal_description: Review Big-O notation, linked lists, stacks, queues, and binary trees. Midterm is 60 minutes MCQ worth 10% of grade, tested directly in the lab session.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Review Big-O notation — be able to give the formal definition and identify the complexity class (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)) of a given algorithm with nested loops.
Task 2: Study the list data structure — implementation using arrays and singly linked lists, and compare their trade-offs.
Task 3: Practice stack and queue operations — push, pop, enqueue, dequeue — and their implementations using both linked lists and arrays.
Task 4: Review applications of stacks (e.g., expression trees) and queues.
Task 5: Study binary tree concepts: basic definitions, storage structures, traversal methods (in-order, pre-order, post-order), binary search trees, and expression trees.
Task 6: Practice tracing the step-by-step execution of BST insert, delete, and search.
Task 7: Complete all in-class exercise sets from sessions 1–4.
Task 8: Take one full 60-minute MCQ practice test covering the above topics.

goal_description: Complete the large programming assignment (BTL) requiring implementation of data structures and algorithms in C++. Assignment is 30% of the total grade and is auto-graded by the system.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Read the full assignment specification carefully and list all required data structures and algorithms.
Task 2: Review C++ fundamentals needed: pointers, arrays, structs, templates, OOP, and exception handling.
Task 3: Implement the required linked list class with all specified methods.
Task 4: Implement the required tree structure (BST or AVL as specified) with insert, delete, search, and traversal.
Task 5: Implement any required sorting algorithm(s) — trace through step-by-step to verify correctness before coding.
Task 6: Implement any required searching or hashing algorithm with the specified collision resolution strategy.
Task 7: Test each component with edge cases: empty structure, single element, duplicate keys, and large inputs.
Task 8: Analyze the Big-O complexity of each implemented method and document it in the report.
Task 9: Submit via the auto-grading system before the deadline and verify all test cases pass.

goal_description: Understand and be able to implement AVL trees, multi-way trees, and B-Trees as covered in sessions 4–5 of the course.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Review basic binary search tree operations and their worst-case complexities before moving to balanced trees.
Task 2: Study AVL tree rotations: single right rotation, single left rotation, right-left rotation, and left-right rotation — trace through 5 examples of each.
Task 3: Practice AVL insert and delete with rebalancing from scratch on paper.
Task 4: Study multi-way trees: definition, properties, and how search and insertion differ from binary trees.
Task 5: Study B-Tree structure: order, minimum/maximum keys per node, split on insert, merge on delete.
Task 6: Practice B-Tree insertion and deletion step-by-step on examples of order 3 and order 4 trees.
Task 7: Compare AVL trees and B-Trees: when to use each, and how their performance characteristics differ.
Task 8: Solve all exercises from the session 4–5 exercise sets.

goal_description: Review lexical specification with regular expressions, context-free grammar with BNF, parse trees, and abstract syntax trees. Midterm is 60 minutes MCQ worth 20% of grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Study regular expression syntax and semantics — practice writing regex for common token types: identifiers, integer literals, float literals, string literals, and operators.
Task 2: Study automata and token identification — understand how a lexer uses a DFA to match tokens.
Task 3: Study context-free grammar and BNF notation — be able to write a grammar for a simple language.
Task 4: Practice constructing parse trees for given strings and grammars.
Task 5: Study ambiguity in grammars — be able to identify ambiguous grammars and resolve them using precedence and associativity rules.
Task 6: Practice writing abstract syntax trees (AST) from parse trees.
Task 7: Complete Large Assignment 1 topics: write lexical and grammar specifications for the assigned simple language.
Task 8: Review all in-class exercises from sessions 2 and 3.
Task 9: Take a 60-minute MCQ practice test under timed conditions.

goal_description: Complete Large Assignment 2 and/or 4 requiring implementation of intermediate code generation or JVM Jasmin code generation for the assigned language. Assignment contributes to the 30% project grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Review the AST structure produced in Assignment 1 — understand each node type and what code it should generate.
Task 2: Study JVM architecture: the operand stack, local variable array, and the instruction set covered in Chapter 10 (Jasmin code).
Task 3: Learn Jasmin assembly syntax: class structure, method descriptors, and the key instructions (iload, istore, iadd, if_icmpeq, invokevirtual, etc.).
Task 4: Implement code generation for arithmetic expressions and assignment statements first.
Task 5: Implement code generation for conditional statements (if-else).
Task 6: Implement code generation for loop constructs.
Task 7: Implement code generation for function/method calls including parameter passing.
Task 8: Run and test generated Jasmin code by assembling and executing it on the JVM.
Task 9: Submit before the deadline — the course requires at least 50% of assignments submitted to avoid being barred from the final exam.

goal_name: Understand Data Types and Control Structures in Programming Languages
goal_description: Master Chapter 8 (Data Types) and Chapter 9 (Control Structures) — key topics for both the midterm and final exam, covering scope, type systems, parameter passing mechanisms.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Study scope rules and reference environments — understand static (lexical) scope vs. dynamic scope with code examples.
Task 2: Study data type concepts: type information, basic types, type constructors (arrays, records, pointers), type equivalence (structural vs. name equivalence), and type checking.
Task 3: Study type conversion: implicit coercion vs. explicit casting.
Task 4: Study data abstraction: abstract data types and their relationship to OOP.
Task 5: Study control structures: expression evaluation order, short-circuit evaluation, conditional statements, and loop constructs.
Task 6: Study parameter passing mechanisms in depth: pass-by-value, pass-by-reference, pass-by-value-result, and pass-by-name — trace examples in C, C++, and Python.
Task 7: Complete Large Assignment 3 (covers mechanisms of scope, reference environment, and data types) before its deadline.
Task 8: Review all in-class exercises from sessions 7, 8, and 9.

goal_description: Review performance metrics, MIPS instruction set architecture, and computer arithmetic. Midterm is 60 minutes MCQ worth 20% of the total grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Study performance metrics: understand CPU execution time, CPI, clock cycle time, and instruction count (IC) — be able to calculate machine performance given these parameters.
Task 2: Learn to distinguish CPI, Clock Cycles, and IC and understand how each contributes to overall performance.
Task 3: Study benchmark types used to evaluate performance (SPEC benchmarks).
Task 4: Study MIPS instruction set architecture: instruction formats (R-type, I-type, J-type), addressing modes, and the register set.
Task 5: Practice interpreting arithmetic, logic, branching, and data transfer instructions in MIPS assembly.
Task 6: Practice translating MIPS assembly instructions into 32-bit machine code (binary and hex).
Task 7: Practice writing simple MIPS subroutines that interact with the user using syscalls.
Task 8: Study binary arithmetic: signed/unsigned number representation, binary addition/subtraction, overflow detection, logic operations, and the ALU design.
Task 9: Take a 60-minute MCQ practice test covering sessions 1–8.

goal_name: Master MIPS Pipeline and Hazard Detection
goal_description: Deeply understand the pipelined data path (sessions 9–12): the 5-stage pipeline, data hazards, control hazards, and structural hazards, as these are heavily tested in the final exam.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Review the single-cycle data path and control signals before studying the pipeline — understand what each stage (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) does.
Task 2: Study the pipelined data path: pipeline registers (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB) and how data flows through them.
Task 3: Study data hazards: identify RAW (Read After Write) hazards in a given code sequence and determine the number of stall cycles needed.
Task 4: Study forwarding/bypassing: understand when forwarding resolves a RAW hazard and when a stall is still required (load-use hazard).
Task 5: Study control hazards: understand branch delay and branch prediction strategies (predict-not-taken, predict-taken).
Task 6: Practice on 5+ assembly code sequences: draw the pipeline diagram, identify all hazards, apply forwarding, and count total cycles.
Task 7: Study structural hazards and how they are typically eliminated in MIPS (e.g., separate instruction and data memory).
Task 8: Solve all exercises from the textbook (Patterson & Hennessy, 5th edition) Chapter 4 on pipeline hazards.

goal_name: Study Memory Hierarchy and Cache Organization
goal_description: Understand cache memory organization (direct-mapped, set-associative, fully-associative), cache sizing calculations, and virtual memory concepts from sessions 13–14 for the final exam.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Study the principle of locality (temporal and spatial) and why it justifies the memory hierarchy.
Task 2: Study direct-mapped cache: understand index bits, tag bits, offset bits, and how to determine which cache block a memory address maps to.
Task 3: Study set-associative cache: understand the difference from direct-mapped, how the set index and tag are computed, and replacement policies (LRU).
Task 4: Study fully-associative cache: compare with the above two methods in terms of hit rate and complexity.
Task 5: Practice calculating cache size: given block size, number of sets, associativity, and address width, calculate total cache capacity and the number of tag/index/offset bits.
Task 6: Study write policies: write-through vs. write-back with write-allocate.
Task 7: Study the relationship between cache memory, main memory (DRAM), and secondary memory — understand miss penalty and average memory access time (AMAT).
Task 8: Study virtual memory: page tables, TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer), and page fault handling.
Task 9: Solve 10+ cache calculation exercises from the textbook and past exams.

goal_name: Prepare for Earth Science Final Exam
goal_description: Review all four spheres (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere/human activities) and their interactions. Final exam is 80 minutes MCQ worth 60% of the grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Review geosphere topics — mineral physical properties and classification, rock cycle (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic rocks and their identification), plate tectonics theory, earthquake types and seismic waves, Earth's interior structure, and geological time scale principles.
Task 2: Review atmosphere topics — atmospheric structure and composition, humidity and precipitation processes, atmospheric circulation (Hadley, Ferrel, Polar cells, Walker cell), climate types, storm formation, and deserts.
Task 3: Review hydrosphere topics — surface water, groundwater (porosity vs. permeability), ocean composition and circulation (gyres, thermocline), tides and waves.
Task 4: Review sphere interactions — climate change mechanisms (greenhouse gases, energy balance, global warming evidence), weathering processes, mass wasting (landslide mechanisms), and the geological time scale.
Task 5: Review Earth resources — mineral, water, and fuel resources (fossil fuels, renewable energy, geothermal).
Task 6: Review topographic maps: coordinate systems, map scale, how to read contour lines, and drawing topographic cross-sections.
Task 7: Complete all e-learning exercises for chapters 1–13 before the exam.
Task 8: Take a full 80-minute MCQ mock exam covering all topics.

goal_description: Submit lab reports for all 5 practice sessions (minerals, igneous rocks, sedimentary/metamorphic rocks, topographic maps, compass use). Lab work counts for 20% of the total grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Practice 1 (Minerals) — identify the physical properties of provided mineral samples (color, luster, hardness, cleavage/fracture, streak) and name each mineral. Write the lab report.
Task 2: Practice 2 (Igneous rocks) — identify the texture and structure of igneous rock samples, classify them as felsic, intermediate, or mafic. Write the lab report.
Task 3: Practice 3 (Sedimentary and metamorphic rocks) — identify texture and structure, classify each rock type. Write the lab report.
Task 4: Practice 4 (Topographic maps) — identify map features (drainage, transportation, vegetation, contour lines), read coordinate systems and map scale, and draw a topographic cross-section for the given profile. Write the lab report.
Task 5: Practice 5 (Compass use and navigation) — locate positions on a topographic map, measure azimuth and dip of fractures/faults/rock layers using the compass. Write the lab report.
Task 6: Submit each lab report at the end of the respective lab session as required by the instructor.
Task 7: Review reports before submission — ensure all identification tables are complete and observations are explained.

goal_name: Write Earth Science Group Report on Climate Change and Earth Resources
goal_description: Complete the group project report (BTL) on the roles of Earth resources or renewable/non-renewable energy in sustainable economic development. Report contributes 20% to the final grade.
ground_truth:
Task 1: Form a group of 5 students and assign roles: team leader, researcher for each sub-topic (atmosphere/climate, resources/energy, impact on society, and conclusion/recommendations).
Task 2: Review course content on climate change: solar radiation balance, greenhouse gases and their effects, global warming evidence, and climate modelling concepts (Chapter 3).
Task 3: Review Earth resources (Chapter 12): mineral resources, water resources, fossil fuels (oil, gas, coal), nuclear energy, and renewable energy sources (solar, wind, tidal, geothermal).
Task 4: Search for at least 3–5 peer-reviewed or reputable sources on the group's chosen topic; summarize each source as part of the basic literature review (L.O.7).
Task 5: Draft the report structure: Introduction → Literature Review → Main Discussion → Conclusion and Recommendations.
Task 6: Write the discussion section connecting climate change evidence to the viability of renewable vs. non-renewable energy in sustainable development.
Task 7: Create the mind-map showing the relationships between Earth Science disciplines relevant to the topic (required deliverable from Week 1, due Week 7).
Task 8: Review and finalize the report — ensure all members' contributions are documented for individual evaluation (L.O.6). Submit before the deadline.
